entry.title: Cheng v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1631
entry.content:
The Federal Court dismissed Ms Cheng’s judicial review application challenging an Administrative Review Tribunal decision that affirmed non-revocation of her visa cancellation under s 501(3A). The Court rejected claims that the Tribunal committed jurisdictional error in its treatment of her drug history, rehabilitation evidence, community expectations and legal consequences. The application was dismissed with costs.

Key holding: HZCP prevents a Tribunal from going behind facts that support the conviction and sentence, but it does not bar consideration of historical facts that did not support the sentence.

So, even if the finding by the sentencing judge is to be construed as a finding that Ms Cheng had never been a drug user, it was only the finding as at the time of offending that supported the sentencing. The principles in HZCP did not concern factual findings that did not support the sentence that was made.

entry.title: Singh v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1638
entry.content:
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from a dismissal of judicial review of a Tribunal decision refusing a partner visa because the appellant did not satisfy Schedule 3 criterion 3001 and the Tribunal was not satisfied there were compelling reasons to waive it. The appellant raised numerous grounds, including new points and late AI-prepared grounds, but the Court refused leave for most new points and dismissed the appeal.

Key holding: In migration appeals, leave to raise a new point not taken below may be granted where it clearly has merit and there is no real prejudice to the respondent, but is generally refused where there is no adequate explanation and the point is of doubtful merit.

Specifically in relation to migration cases, where an adverse decision may have various serious consequences for an appellant, the Court may grant leave to raise such a new point that was not taken below if the point clearly has merit and there is no real prejudice to the respondent in permitting it to be agitated.

entry.title: Arias v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1903
entry.content:
This case concerned two out-of-time judicial review applications by a Colombian citizen challenging ART decisions affirming the cancellation of his Bridging C (Subclass 030) visa and the refusal of his Partner (Temporary) (Subclass 820) visa. The Court refused both extensions of time because the proposed grounds had no reasonable prospects of success and ordered costs in each matter.

Key holding: Under s 477(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), an extension of time should be refused where the proposed grounds of judicial review have no prospects of success.

Where there are no prospects of the applicant's grounds of review succeeding, an extension is to be refused.

entry.title: Boleno & Newcombe [2026] FedCFamC1A 191
entry.content:
This was an appeal by a father against final parenting orders requiring his time with the child to be professionally supervised until she turns 10, after the primary judge found he posed an unacceptable risk of psychological harm. The appellate court dismissed the appeal, holding that no relevant error was established, and made costs orders against the appellant.

Key holding: In determining whether a parent poses an unacceptable risk of future harm, a court may rely on findings about past conduct and present insight as the foundation for the predictive assessment.

Furthermore, the predictive exercise of risk assessment cannot be undertaken other than by reference to past events.

entry.title: FDB17 v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1612
entry.content:
The appellant, a Pakistani protection visa applicant, appealed a Federal Circuit and Family Court judgment dismissing his judicial review application concerning an AAT decision that affirmed refusal of his visa. He argued the Tribunal fell into jurisdictional error by unreasonably declining to telephone four corroborating witnesses (his parents, brother and a friend) who had already provided a joint signed statement. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal, holding the Tribunal's approach had a rational and intelligible foundation.

Key holding: Where a decision-maker is convinced that an applicant's account is fabricated or fundamentally unreliable, it is not irrational or illogical to decline to hear oral corroborating evidence and to reject that corroboration, even absent any independent ground for doubting the corroborators.

It is not necessarily irrational, or illogical, for a finder of fact, who is convinced that a principal witness is fabricating a story, which is considered to be inherently implausible, to reject corroborative evidence, even though there is no separate or independent ground for its rejection, apart from the reasons given for disbelieving the principal witness.

entry.title: Rangel & Bird (No 2) [2026] FedCFamC1A 193
entry.content:
This was a mother’s appeal against three parenting orders concerning the children’s international travel, passports and extra-curricular activities. The appellate court found the primary judge denied procedural fairness by making orders materially outside the case presented by the parties and the Independent Children’s Lawyer. The appeal was allowed, the relevant orders were set aside, and the discretion was re-exercised.

Key holding: Procedural fairness ordinarily requires that parties be given an opportunity to address an order materially outside the range of orders sought or reasonably anticipated, and breach is appealable where material.

While a primary judge is not bound by the parties' and the ICL's proposals ( U v U [2002] HCA 36 ; (2002) 211 CLR 238) , procedural fairness ordinarily requires that the parties be afforded an opportunity to address a course materially outside the range of orders sought or reasonably anticipated ( Duarte & Morse [2019] FamCAFC 93 ; (2019) FLC 93-902).

entry.title: Jamdar v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1620
entry.content:
The Federal Court granted an extension of time but dismissed an appeal from the Administrative Review Tribunal, which had affirmed refusal of Australian citizenship by conferral on good-character grounds. The applicant challenged the Tribunal’s treatment of earlier non-conviction offending and its finding that he deliberately withheld his 2023 conviction.

Key holding: Part VIIC of the Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) precludes reliance on the fact of a charge, conviction or finding of guilt, but does not preclude an administrative decision-maker from considering the underlying conduct.

Sections 85ZR and 85ZS are directed to the fact of a charge, conviction or finding of guilt and do not expressly preclude an administrative decision-maker from considering the underlying conduct.

entry.title: Kearney v Migration Agents Registration Authority [2026] FCA 1615
entry.content:
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from a Tribunal decision affirming cancellation of a migration agent’s registration for five years under s 303(1)(a) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the agent breached the Code of Conduct and was not a fit and proper person, based on nomination applications lodged for nine businesses without their knowledge or permission. Dowling J dismissed the appeal.

Key holding: Under the former reg 3(1) definition, a migration agent’s client includes any person to whom the agent agrees to provide immigration assistance, even without a retainer or the person’s express or implied acceptance.

I agree with the Authority's submissions and accept that 'client', as it was defined by reg 3(1) of the Regulations at the time of the applicant's conduct in question, includes persons to whom a registered migration agent agrees to provide immigration assistance even in the absence of a retainer or where the recipient of the assistance has not expressly or impliedly agreed to receive it.

entry.title: Roseingrave v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1602
entry.content:
The Federal Court reviewed a Tribunal decision affirming the non-revocation of Mr Roseingrave’s visa cancellation. The Court upheld two grounds because the Tribunal treated Direction 110’s cll 8.3 and 8.4 as exhaustive and failed to evaluate his representations about the impact on his wife and son. The third ground concerning asserted Torres Strait ties failed.

Key holding: The limits of the primary considerations in Direction 110 do not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by a visa cancellation review applicant.

The correct identification of the limits of the primary considerations referred to in Direction 110 did not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by Mr Roseingrave.

entry.title: Fred-Tutavaha v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1586
entry.content:
The applicant, a New Zealand citizen who arrived in Australia aged four, sought judicial review of the Assistant Minister's decision under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to set aside an AAT decision revoking the cancellation of his visa. He ran three grounds — unreasonable delay, failure to consider immigration detention as a legal consequence, and legal unreasonableness in giving legal consequences "neutral weight" — with the Court also considering a proposed fourth ground on the national interest assessment.

Key holding: A failure to refer expressly to immigration detention in reasons for a s 501BA cancellation does not permit an inference that this legal consequence was not considered, where detention pending removal is an obvious and well-known statutory consequence and there is no barrier to removal.

It does not follow, however, that the proper inference is that the Assistant Minister failed to appreciate that a legal consequence of his decision was that the Applicant would be taken into immigration detention. The statement of reasons must be read fairly and as a whole, and the fact that a matter is not mentioned expressly does not necessarily mean it was not considered

entry.title: Fotu v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1589
entry.content:
The Federal Court set aside the Assistant Minister’s personal decision under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to override an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and cancel Mr Fotu’s visa. The determinative error was the Minister’s illogical dismissal as “untenable” of the relevance of the applicant’s youth and developing maturity to the risk of reoffending. The decision was quashed on judicial review.

Key holding: Dismissing as “untenable” the evidence-supported relevance of a young offender’s developing maturity to reoffending risk is illogical or irrational and can constitute material jurisdictional error.

I do not consider a logical or rational person would have reached a conclusion that it was untenable to have regard to the applicant's maturity over time in the face of the available evidence.

entry.title: Harvey v State of Queensland [2026] QCA 214
entry.content:
The Queensland Court of Appeal dismissed Mr Harvey’s appeal from a decision refusing to set aside his notice of discontinuance of a police assault damages claim filed more than seven years earlier. The Court found no error in the primary judge’s discretionary conclusion that the appellant had not shown good reason, or that the interests of justice required, setting aside the discontinuance, given unparticularised evidence and unexplained delay.

Key holding: Even if a court may set aside a notice of discontinuance where the interests of justice require it, unparticularised claims of duress or mental illness and lengthy unexplained delay will not satisfy that test.

Assuming in the appellant's favour that the court had power to set aside the discontinuance if it was shown to be in the interests of justice to do so, the material before the primary judge did not satisfy that test.

entry.title: Kola v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1550
entry.content:
The Federal Court dismissed Mr Kola’s challenge to an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal of citizenship by conferral under s 21(2)(h) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth). The Court upheld the Tribunal’s finding that his criminal history outweighed remorse, rehabilitation evidence and a low risk of reoffending.

Key holding: A low risk of future offending does not by itself establish that a person is presently of good character under s 21(2)(h).

An assessment that a person presents a low risk of future offending is not equivalent to a conclusion that the person is presently of good character within the meaning of s 21(2)(h).

entry.title: Darlington-Thomas v Elgas Limited [2026] FCA 1566
entry.content:
The Federal Court granted Ms Darlington-Thomas leave under s 46PO(3A)(a) of the Australian Human Rights Commission Act 1986 (Cth) to proceed against her labour hire employer, Zoom, for alleged disability discrimination. The AHRC had terminated her complaint against Zoom, but the Court held the claim was reasonably arguable and should be resolved with the overlapping claim against Elgas.

Key holding: On an application for leave under s 46PO(3A)(a) of the AHRC Act, the Court asks only whether the proposed discrimination claim is reasonably arguable and not fanciful, rather than determining the merits.

I am satisfied that the text, context and purpose of the leave requirement in s 46PO(3A) suggests that it is appropriate for the Court to consider in determining whether to grant leave whether the claims made by an applicant are reasonably arguable, and are - at the least - not fanciful. This is consistent with the language used in s 46P(1A).

entry.title: Hormaza v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1925
entry.content:
The applicant sought judicial review of an ART decision affirming refusal of a student visa for failing to meet English language proficiency requirements. He alleged procedural unfairness, his migration agent’s negligence, legal unreasonableness, and the ART’s use of the wrong legislative instrument. The Court dismissed the application, finding no jurisdictional error and that the instrument error was immaterial.

Key holding: A representative’s negligence or administrative error in failing to notify an applicant of a hearing does not, without fraud or dishonesty, vitiate the Tribunal’s decision.

As stated in DUA16 at [15], "an administrative decision [under the Act] is not vitiated merely by bad or negligent advice or some other mishap that leads to detriment to an applicant", including negligence by a representative.

entry.title: Watson v Director of Public Prosecutions (NSW) [2026] NSWCA 222
entry.content:
Mr Watson sought judicial review in the NSW Court of Appeal of Beckett DCJ’s refusal under s 5B of the Criminal Appeal Act 1912 (NSW) to submit questions of law to the Court of Criminal Appeal after his conviction appeal was dismissed. The Court of Appeal dismissed the amended summons, holding that no jurisdictional error was shown in her Honour’s treatment of the proposed questions. Costs were awarded to the DPP.

Key holding: On judicial review of a s 5B decision, an error by the District Court in characterising a proposed question as law, fact or mixed fact and law is ordinarily an error of law within jurisdiction and therefore not a jurisdictional error.

As a consequence, an error by a judge, when determining an application under s 5B, in characterising a proposed question as a question of law, a question of fact, or a question of mixed law and fact, is ordinarily apt to be characterised as an error of law within jurisdiction.

entry.title: BNE24 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1561
entry.content:
This was an appeal from the Federal Circuit and Family Court (Division 2) dismissing review of a Tribunal decision refusing a protection visa. The unrepresented appellant argued the Tribunal’s adverse credibility findings were illogical or unreasonable. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal, holding the primary judge correctly found no jurisdictional error.

Key holding: A Tribunal’s adverse credibility finding does not involve jurisdictional error merely because a reviewing court would have reached a different factual finding; the reasoning must be legally unreasonable.

Therefore, jurisdictional error in the reasoning by the Tribunal as to the credibility of the account given by an applicant is not established by seeking to persuade a court on review that the Tribunal's reasoning includes an error in the sense that the Court would not make the same finding.

entry.title: Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson [2026] FCA 1548
entry.content:
SXHR, a Sri Lankan unauthorised maritime arrival in immigration detention, sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Bridging E visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal had applied Direction No 110 and refused the visa notwithstanding the applicant’s outstanding Ministerial intervention request. The Federal Court dismissed the review.

Key holding: Direction 110 requires comparison of the risk attached to refusal and grant of the visa, but not separate assessment of every possible outcome after grant where only the grant creates a risk of the applicant remaining in the community.

There is no error in that approach; nothing could have been gained by comparing the nature or extent of that risk depending on which of the two identified scenarios following the grant of a visa eventuated. DVRL does not say anything against that.

entry.title: Barresi v Cross Yarra Partnerships [2026] VSC 666
entry.content:
The plaintiff sought judicial review of a second Wrongs Act Medical Panel determination that his whole person impairment did not meet the threshold, after an earlier panel had found that it did. The Court followed Citywide Service Solutions Pty Ltd v Rosata in permitting the later panel to determine the same medical question, and rejected the challenge based on s 28LZG(4). The catchwords record “Appeal dismissed”.

Key holding: An asserted misunderstanding by a Medical Panel of s 28LZG(4) will not constitute jurisdictional error unless the misunderstanding was material to the determination, in the sense that the decision could realistically have been different.

Consequently, in my opinion, the plaintiff has not established that the asserted misunderstanding by the second Panel of s 28LZG(4) was material to the decision that the second Panel made and therefore jurisdictional error has not been established.

entry.title: GWN25 by his Litigation Representative the Public Advocate v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1535
entry.content:

This is a costs judgment following the Full Court’s earlier decision in Chukwuma v Assistant Minister for Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCAFC 121. The appellant succeeded on the appeal but failed on two interlocutory applications. The Court ordered the respondent to pay 85% of the appellant’s appeal costs, applying an issues-based percentage discount.

Key holding: Where an appeal succeeds overall but the appellant fails on discrete interlocutory applications, the Court may adopt an issues-based approach and apply a percentage discount to costs rather than making separate costs orders for each issue.

In our view, in the present case, it is appropriate: to adopt an "issues based" approach; to view the two interlocutory applications as separate issues; and to have regard to the success or failure of the parties on the issues.

entry.title: OZY25 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1983
entry.content:
The applicants sought judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal of Subclass 866 protection visas. They alleged jurisdictional error arising from their former representative’s conduct, which they said caused an uninformed request for a decision on the papers and stultified the statutory review process. The Federal Circuit and Family Court dismissed the application, finding the factual foundation for the alleged stultification was not proved.

Key holding: A claim that representative conduct affected the validity of a Tribunal decision requires proof of the alleged failure and its disabling effect; it cannot be inferred merely from hindsight that a hearing might have offered forensic advantages.

Whatever duties s 56 may impose upon a representative, a failure capable of affecting the validity of the Tribunal's decision must first be proved. Section 56 does not permit the Court to infer deficient advice merely from the fact that, with hindsight, attendance might have offered additional forensic opportunities.

entry.title: Guo v Hu [2026] NSWDC 368
entry.content:
In Guo v Hu [2026] NSWDC 368, the plaintiff sought to set aside or restrict inspection of documents produced by the Department of Home Affairs under a subpoena issued by the defendant in a contractual dispute over share repurchase and a $150,000 investment. The District Court declined to set aside the subpoena entirely but, under UCPR r 33.9(3), limited access to migration documents capable of bearing on the pleaded issues, with a schedule to divide Access Granted and Access Refused documents. Costs were costs in the cause.

Key holding: Where subpoenaed documents have been produced but only some are apparently relevant, the court may refuse to set aside the subpoena and instead restrict inspection under UCPR r 33.9(3) to documents bearing on pleaded issues, refusing access to irrelevant personal material.

The Court's task under r 33.9 is not confined to a binary choice between complete access and no access. There is no reason why restricted access orders cannot properly be made where documents contain confidential or highly personal information and where only part of the material bears upon matters genuinely in dispute.

entry.title: JACOBS -v- HER HONOUR MAGISTRATE WARD [2026] WASC 435
entry.content:
Ms Jacobs, a public housing tenant, sought judicial review of a Magistrates Court decision dismissing her Residential Tenancies Act claims and finding no jurisdiction over her Australian Consumer Law claims. The Supreme Court found a reasonably arguable case and identified jurisdictional errors arising from denial of natural justice and misconstruction of RTA provisions. The decision was quashed in part and remitted to the Magistrates Court, differently constituted.

Key holding: On judicial review under s 36 MCA and s 26(2) RTA, an inferior court’s decision is affected by jurisdictional error only where it fails to exercise judicial power itself, including by misconceiving its statutory function or power, rather than merely making an error within jurisdiction.

These cases confirm that the relevant inquiry upon an application for judicial review of a decision of an inferior court is whether there has been a failure of the judicial officer to exercise judicial power itself or whether the judicial officer has merely made an error while exercising that judicial power. The former will generally constitute jurisdictional error; the latter will not.

entry.title: Cristobal Fida v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1471

The applicant sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Working Holiday visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) due to character concerns. The Federal Court allowed the application, finding the Tribunal misapplied Direction 110 by assessing substantive visa eligibility rather than whether the duration and purpose of the intended stay affected risk of harm to the Australian community. The Tribunal decision was quashed and the matter remitted for determination according to law.

Key holding: Under Direction 110 [8.1.2(2)(c)], the Tribunal must consider whether and how the duration and purpose of an intended stay affect risk of harm to the Australian community, not whether the applicant satisfies substantive visa eligibility criteria.

The Tribunal erred by misapprehending the nature of the inquiry. entry.title: RSZN v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1467

This wording introduces a higher subjective mental element and means that the accessory must have lent his or her assistance with the aim of facilitating the offence. entry.title: EMO25 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1950
entry.content:
The applicants sought an extension of time to challenge an ART decision that it lacked jurisdiction over their protection visa review because their AAT review application was lodged one day late. The Court refused the extension, finding the underlying judicial review had no merit because the old review-period law applied. The delay was only six days, but the ART’s jurisdictional conclusion was correct.

Key holding: The new ART review-period rule in s 347(3)(b) does not apply retrospectively to applications filed before its commencement; earlier lodgements remain governed by the old law.

While item 24 in sch 16 to the Administrative Review Tribunal (Consequential and Transitional Provisions No. 1) Act 2024 (Cth) makes clear proceedings that had already commenced in the Tribunal would be continued under the new provisions in the ART, there is no reason to suppose s 347(3)(b) applied retroactively to applications filed prior to the commencement of that provision.

entry.title: ANF26 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1949
entry.content:
The applicant, a Malaysian citizen who claimed protection because he is gay, sought judicial review after the Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed refusal of his protection visa. He filed 17 days outside the 35-day period and needed an extension under s 477(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Court refused the extension because the proposed judicial review application lacked sufficient merit, notwithstanding the relatively short delay and absence of specific prejudice.

Key holding: On a s 477(2) extension application, an underlying judicial review application lacking merit can decisively weigh against an extension even where the delay is short and no specific prejudice is shown.

When I weigh the considerations, I am unable to be satisfied it is necessary in the interests of the administration of justice to extend the time for making the application for review. The absence of merit in the underlying application weighs decisively against granting an extension of time.

entry.title: BYQ21 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1948
entry.content:
The applicant sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Protection (Class XA) (Subclass 866) visa, having claimed Taliban-related risk in Pakistan. The Court found no jurisdictional error and dismissed the application.

Key holding: Where a tribunal finds no real chance of serious harm in an applicant’s home area, it is not required to assess the difficulties of internal relocation.

The Tribunal did not need to consider the difficulties the applicant might face if he were forced to relocate to another part of the country because it was satisfied in all the circumstances that the applicant would not face undue risk if he returned to Swat, his home: see [51]-[54].

entry.title: BFK21 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1947
entry.content:
The Court dismissed BFK21’s judicial review challenge to a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a protection visa. The Tribunal had disbelieved the applicant’s claims of Christian conversion and feared persecution in China, relying on delay, inconsistencies and absence of corroboration. The Court found no jurisdictional error and dismissed the application.

Key holding: Delay in applying for protection is a legitimate factual consideration, and a rational basis, for assessing the genuineness or depth of an alleged fear of persecution.

In my opinion, this was a legitimate factual argument and an obvious one to take into account in assessing the genuineness, or at least the depth, of the applicant's alleged fear of persecution. It is a rational consideration open on the material.

entry.title: Kaur v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1944
entry.content:
The applicant sought reinstatement of her judicial review application after it was dismissed for failing to appear at a case management hearing. The Court refused reinstatement because she had no reasonable excuse for non-attendance and her substantive grounds had no reasonable prospects. She was ordered to pay $2,500 costs, with the earlier $3,850 costs order remaining extant.

Key holding: On an application to reinstate a judicial review proceeding, the MZYEZ considerations are not mandatory; the Court exercises its discretion by reference to the interests of justice.

The Full Court of the Federal Court has made clear that these are not mandatory relevant considerations but potential aspects of what is in the interests of justice in a particular case: FBS18 v Minister for Home Affairs [2019] FCAFC 196 at [53].

entry.title: ANP22 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1943
entry.content:
This was an application for judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming the refusal of Protection (subclass 866) visas to a married Jordanian couple. The applicants claimed protection based on alleged honour-based harm arising from their marriage. The Federal Circuit and Family Court dismissed the application, finding no jurisdictional error, and ordered costs against the applicants.

Key holding: On judicial review under s 476, the Court is confined to jurisdictional error and cannot review the merits of the Tribunal’s decision.

The Court is not permitted to conduct a merits review of the Tribunal decision when reviewing it: see Djokovic v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship, Migrant Services and Multicultural Affairs (2022) 289 FCR 21.

entry.title: DHZ23 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1942
entry.content:
The applicant sought judicial review under s 476 of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Protection (subclass 866) visa. The Tribunal rejected the applicant’s claims concerning forced demolition, compensation and alleged past harm, finding no well-founded fear of persecution or real risk of significant harm. The Court found no jurisdictional error and dismissed the application with fixed costs.

Key holding: Mere disagreement with a Tribunal’s factual findings does not establish jurisdictional error on judicial review.

To the extent that the Applicant's submissions amount to disagreement with the Tribunal's findings, mere disagreement does not establish jurisdictional error: see Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs v Eshetu [1999] HCA 21; (1999) 197 CLR 611 at [40] per Gleeson CJ and McHugh J and Vo v Minister for Home Affairs [2019] FCAFC 108; (2019) 269 FCR 566 per Derrington, Banks-Smith and Colvin JJ.

entry.title: GFT26 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1940
entry.content:
This was an application under s 256 of the FCFCOA Act for review of a Registrar’s summary dismissal of the applicant’s judicial review proceeding. The applicant had sought review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a protection visa, but he told the Department and Tribunal that his protection claims were false and that he did not fear harm in Malaysia. The Court dismissed the review and upheld the summary dismissal with costs.

Key holding: Summary dismissal is appropriate where there is no real or genuine dispute that might reasonably be resolved in the applicant’s favour, as distinct from merely asserting jurisdictional error.

This involves a consideration of whether the case raises a real or genuine dispute that might reasonably be resolved in the applicant's favour, as distinct from identification of jurisdictional error in the Tribunal's decision: AJB19 v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship, Migrant Services and Multicultural Affairs [2021] FedCFamC2G 368 (AJB19) per Judge Given at [33] and the cases cited therein.

entry.title: Chen v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1939
entry.content:
The applicant sought judicial review under s 476 of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) of a Tribunal decision affirming cancellation of her student visa under s 116(1)(g), based on her conviction for concealing a serious indictable offence. She alleged the Tribunal constructively failed to consider claims about low reoffending risk and respect for immigration law, and exceeded its function by going beyond the District Court conviction and sentence. The Court dismissed the application with costs.

Key holding: A decision-maker may consider conduct beyond the elements of the offence, but cannot rely on evidence contrary to the essential facts establishing the conviction or sentence where that conviction or sentence is the jurisdictional foundation.

I concur with the Minister's submission that the ratio of this case is that where the conviction or sentence is the foundation for the decision maker's jurisdiction, it would be an error for the Tribunal to rely upon evidence that is contrary to the essential conviction or sentencing facts: HZCP at [78].
